scenes.narration: Nothing in Welcome to the N.H.K. was built for you — it was built for reproduction. Welcome to the N.H.K. (Japanese: N・H・Kにようこそ!, Hepburn: N.H.K. ni Yōkoso!) is a Japanese novel   written by Tatsuhiko Takimoto. It was published by Kadokawa Shoten in Japan in January 2002, and in English by Tokyopop in October 2007.

The psychology underneath Welcome to the N.H.K. is simpler and older than the story on top. The story revolves around Tatsuhiro Sato, a 22-year-old hikikomori, an asocial recluse, who gets aid from a strange girl who seems to know a lot about him, despite never having met him before. Common themes throughout the story deal with depression, anxiety, isolation, existential dread, the hardships of life and how people must deal with them in their own way.

Behind Welcome to the N.H.K. sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. The novel profusely analyzes the hikikomori phenomenon, which is relatively widespread in Japan. Welcome to the N.H.K. was adapted into a manga series, also written by Takimoto, with art by Kendi Oiwa.

The nihilist does not deny Welcome to the N.H.K. — he only refuses to flatter it. The manga was serialized between June 2004 and June 2007 in Kadokawa Shoten's manga magazine Shōnen Ace. The manga's forty chapters have been collected into eight bound volumes released in Japan and overseas.

What culture calls destiny in Welcome to the N.H.K. is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. The English edition of the manga is published by Tokyopop, and the first volume was released in October 2006. The novel was also adapted into a 24-episode anime television series by Gonzo which aired in Japan between July and December 2006 on Chiba TV.

The genes do not care about Welcome to the N.H.K.; they care about copies. In North America, the series was licensed for English release by ADV Films, who released it on DVD in 2007. In 2008, the anime became one of over 30 ADV titles acquired by Funimation.

Take away the meaning and Welcome to the N.H.K. still functions — that is the disturbing part. While it mainly deals with the phenomenon of hikikomori, the plot also explores many other Japanese subcultures—for example otaku, lolicon, and Internet suicide pacts. Welcome to the N.H.K. revolves around the lives of several young adults all living in or around the city of Tokyo.

The unconscious does not argue with Welcome to the N.H.K.; it simply acts first. Many different lifestyles are shown though most of the time the story focuses on the concepts of being a hikikomori (a reclusive individual who withdraws from society), anime otaku, and having most of the characters experience intense feelings of depression and loneliness. The main protagonist is Tatsuhiro Satō, a university dropout entering his fourth year of unemployment.

Welcome to the N.H.K. feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. He leads a reclusive life as a hikikomori, ultimately coming to the conclusion that this happened due to some sort of conspiracy. One day, just when his life seems entirely unchanging, he meets Misaki Nakahara, a mysterious girl who claims to be able to cure Tatsuhiro of his hikikomori ways.

The bleak reading of Welcome to the N.H.K. is also the most testable one. She presents him with a contract which states that once a day they would meet in the evening in a local park where Misaki would lecture to Tatsuhiro in an effort to rid him of his lifestyle. During these outings, many subjects are discussed, though they almost always pertain in some way to psychology or psychoanalysis.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Welcome to the N.H.K.. One of their first meetings in fact deals with interpreting Tatsuhiro's recent dreams. Both Tatsuhiro and Misaki, however, have a tendency of over-doing things, such as hiding the truth, especially from each other and themselves.

The self that experiences Welcome to the N.H.K. is a committee, not a king. Despite Misaki's offer and pressing attempts at salvation, it is Tatsuhiro's neighbor and high school friend, Kaoru Yamazaki, whom Tatsuhiro often turns to in moments of need and support. Despite his own idiosyncrasies, Yamazaki is one of the more stable characters in the story.

Reproduction explains more of Welcome to the N.H.K. than any philosophy dares to admit. The plots within the novel, manga and anime are each rather different from one another, and many themes and personalities differ between each. The novel also regularly mentions drug use by the main character, and later, his friend, Yamazaki.

Once you see Welcome to the N.H.K. as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. This element of the story is downplayed in the manga (drugs Satō uses are referred to as "legal psychedelics purchased off the internet"), and, asides alcohol, left out of the story altogether in the anime (with the exception of Hitomi). This is likely due to several reasons, including a more public-friendly rating, as well as ultimately being unneeded for the progression of the plot.

The story Welcome to the N.H.K. tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. The references to lolicon that are present within the novel and manga have also been downplayed within the anime, where most of the women the characters lust after are of mature age, although brief hints still remain. The Nihon Hikikomori Kyōkai (N.H.K.) (日本ひきこもり協会) of Satō's imagination is supposedly a sinister conspiracy which aims to turn people into hikikomori and NEETs.

Meaning is not found in Welcome to the N.H.K. — it is manufactured for it. No clear reason why they would do this is offered, although Satō considers the potential of an "army" of displaced individuals, and it is mentioned that hikikomori are created for the purpose of giving society someone to look down upon, making themselves feel superior. The majority of the N.H.K.'s work is done through the media, via broadcasting anime and other material that is likely to turn the viewer into an otaku.

The cold light on Welcome to the N.H.K. leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. Throughout the series, many shots of advertising hoardings or movie posters incidentally displayed in other locations bear N.H.K. references. Satō on occasion also believes that the N.H.K. takes a more active role via the use of agents, although of course these agents only appear in dream sequences or flashbacks.

Welcome to the N.H.K. did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. Three types of N.H.K. agents are seen: the first are classic Men in Black who appear to have the ability to disguise themselves as anyone else they wish. Satō at one point fears that Misaki may be an agent of this type.

The honest version of Welcome to the N.H.K. starts by giving up the comforting part. The final type of agents are bizarre goblin-like creatures who are grey all over but for a letter (usually "N", "H" or "K") written in yellow on their belly. These creatures appear to be the masterminds of the entire N.H.K. conspiracy, but more likely than not they are Satō's mental image of the spreading mindset or circumstances he associates with the N.H.K.

Strip Welcome to the N.H.K. of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. In the novel, it is hinted that Tatsuhiro may not actually believe the conspiracy to exist but instead needed an imaginary enemy to vent his frustrations on and to help motivate him into overcoming his hikikomori ways. The real-life public broadcaster NHK, which is the source of the abbreviation that is parodied by the series, really does provide a support website for real-life hikikomori.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Welcome to the N.H.K. shows exactly where that breaks. This may have been because the anime was broadcast on TV channels operated by other Japanese broadcasting companies, thus implying that it related to the real TV company and could have been interpreted as slander against a competitor. Puru Puru Pururin (プルプルプルリン) is a fictitious magical girl anime of which Kaoru Yamazaki is a fan, featured only in the anime version (in the novel, Yamazaki is a fan of the real-world show Ojamajo Doremi, which is replaced by Puru Puru Pururin in the anime).

What looks like free choice in Welcome to the N.H.K. is older than choice itself. It is never explicitly stated, but strongly suggested, that Satō believes this series to be controlled by the N.H.K.; in fact, it is after seeing an episode of the series which inspires him to think up the N.H.K. as a concept. For example, although it appears to be a children's style of series, the schedule on the website suggested that it is shown almost daily in the small hours of the morning, when children would not be awake, but hikikomori frequently are.

Nobody designed the part of Welcome to the N.H.K. you experience — it was inherited. The listed broadcast times and channels are in fact the times at which the Welcome to the N.H.K. anime aired.
